strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing genuine limitations of windowed self-attention operators (SCOT) in PDE learning, with clear articulation of drift issues in long-horizon rollouts
Principled dual-branch architecture with sound physical justification (low-k modes for large scales, high-k for fine details) and elegant bandwise radial gating mechanism

Rigorous controlled evaluation following POSEIDON protocol with identical training conditions, consistent improvements across all benchmarks (7-54% error reduction), and long-horizon robustness evaluation (T=100)
Significant efficiency gains: 15% fewer parameters and 34% higher throughput (158 vs 118 steps/s) while improving accuracy
Comprehensive ablation studies with spectral analysis revealing scale-dependent contributions of each component (LFM, RG, FWL)

Theoretical grounding including Lipschitz bounds (Proposition A.2) proving DRIFT has smaller worst-case gain than Swin blocks, energy non-expansiveness proof (Lemma A.3), and connection to discrete Grönwall inequality
Detailed reproducibility: comprehensive pseudocode, implementation details in appendices, code availability promised, and clear presentation with effective figures
weaknesses: Severely limited evaluation scope: only 2D flows tested on narrow class (Navier-Stokes variants); no evaluation on diverse PDEs (diffusion, waves, conservation laws, shock-dominated problems) undermining foundation model claims

Task-specific hyperparameter tuning: low-frequency mask cutoff is hand-tuned initially; no systematic sensitivity analysis or principled guidance for practitioners on new problems, undermining modularity and reusability claims

Modest improvements on several benchmarks: only 7.2% on FNS-KF, 14% on NS-SL compared to 53.6% on NS-PwC, raising questions about what makes tasks different and whether improvements are within statistical noise

Limited baseline comparisons: primary comparison against only SCOT; missing comparisons to PDE-Refiner (which also addresses drift), recent spectral variants (Geo-FNO, CNO), and other multi-scale approaches

Theoretical bounds are loose and disconnect from practice: bounds are relative (vs. Swin blocks) not absolute; condition in Prop. A.2 difficult to verify empirically; unconstrained W lacks spectral-norm clipping despite stability claims

Incomplete analysis of design choices: no ablation for radial vs. hard-band vs. learned non-radial gating; frequency-weighted loss appears orthogonal to main contribution; no visualization of learned mixer weights or mask boundaries

Scalability concerns inadequately addressed: FFT overhead acknowledged as problematic on large grids but not empirically evaluated; no timing breakdown or memory analysis; 3D extension deferred to future work
Missing statistical rigor: no error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests; no reporting of multiple runs or variance; improvements on smaller errors lack quantified uncertainty

Limited generalization evidence: evaluation on smooth/mildly non-smooth problems only; qualitative visualizations acknowledged as cherry-picked; no systematic test on shock-dominated or highly discontinuous regimes

strengths: Clear motivation addressing a real limitation in windowed-attention operators: weak global spectral coupling leading to error drift in long-horizon rollouts
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 7 POSEIDON benchmarks plus 2 ApeBench variants, covering parabolic, hyperbolic, and elliptic PDEs
Consistent empirical improvements (7-54% error reduction) with concurrent gains in efficiency (15% fewer parameters, higher throughput)
Rigorous ablation studies demonstrating each component contributes meaningfully, with spectral analysis of error evolution across frequency bands
Theoretical grounding through Lipschitz bounds, energy non-expansiveness guarantees, and Sobolev-weighted defect bounds
Excellent reproducibility: detailed pseudocode, comprehensive hyperparameters, fixed seeds, documented hardware setup, promise of code release
Modular design enabling easy replacement of windowed attention in existing architectures; practical for integration into PDE foundation models
Long-horizon evaluation with error-growth analysis and comparison across multiple metrics (final error, mean error, error-growth slope)
weaknesses: Limited novelty: combines existing techniques (low-frequency masking, radial gating, frequency-weighted losses) without significant methodological innovation
Scope limited to 2D flows at 128×128 resolution despite framing as general PDE operator; no 3D results or exploration despite acknowledging it as limitation
Variable improvement magnitudes (7-54% across benchmarks) without characterization of problem structure or conditions favoring DRIFT, raising generalization concerns
Handcrafted design choices requiring task-specific tuning: initial low-frequency mask cutoff is hand-tuned, learnable parameters κx, κy have limited flexibility
FFT computational overhead at every block adds memory traffic and latency; acknowledged as limiting for 'very large grids'; resolution scaling shows prohibitive costs at 256×256
Theoretical analysis is motivational rather than deep: Lipschitz bounds are loose with unknown constants and don't provide actionable insights into why coupling improves

Limited baseline comparisons for neural operator work: primarily compares against scOT (strong but single baseline); missing comparisons with other recent spectral-spatial hybrids or modern foundation models
Long-horizon evaluation (T=100) restricted to Kolmogorov flows; error curves show convergence to scOT near horizon end—unclear behavior beyond T=100
Frequency-weighted loss contribution smaller than architectural components in ablations; unclear if redundant with bandwise fusion or well-integrated
Only 2D evaluation despite being positioned as foundational work; cross-resolution testing only at nearby resolutions (64, 96, 128)
